newsitem.title: ANTIGUA AND BARBUDA: Trade issues dominate CARICOM meeting this week.
newsitem.headline: Trade issues dominate CARICOM meeting this week.

text.p: The 14-member Caribbean Community goes into this week's summit meeting facing the daunting task of preparing for simultaneous trade talks with its nearest neighbours in the region, the European Union and all of Latin America.

"Never before as a region have we had to undertake so many complex negotiations simultaneously," Jamaica Prime Minister P.J. Patterson said recently. "When we draw attention to the necessity of transitional (trade) arrangements, we face obduracy and resistance."

When the meeting begins on Wednesay, the regional group will also debate a proposal to replace the British privy council with a Caribbean court of appeals, as well as a plan to review talks with Washington over a series of controversial drug interdiction accords.

At Caricom's meeting in Jamaica last September, heads of government agreed to appoint a sort of trade supremo -- someone of ambassadorial rank who would coordinate technical studies and negotiations on a wide range of upcoming trade talks. The government leaders are expected to formally name former Barbadian Prime Minister Sir Bernard St. John to the post when they meet on Feb. 20-21, according sources close to Caricom.

St. John will oversee Caricom's efforts to achieve equal duty treatment with Mexico in the U.S. market, negotiate its entry into the Free Trade Agreement of the Americas and finalise proposed free trade accords with the Dominican Republic, Colombia, Venezuela, Mercosur and possibly Cuba. He will also oversee discussions with the European Union on the next Lome trade-and-aid accord that begins at the end of this decade.
To improve dialogue with its neighbours, Caricom has invited Haiti's President Rene Preval and Dominican President Lionel Fernandez to attend the Antigua summit.

However, several trade issues have proven problematic for the region. Caricom has lobbied for years, without success, to get Congress to give it duty parity with Mexico on a range of goods, such as apparel.

The region wants a 20-year duty phased out for smaller economies under the FTAA, instead of the proposed 10-year period, and faces not only a reduction in the total Lome package but also the possibility of having to share it with additional Caribbean and African recipients.

"Time is not on the Caribbean's side," David Jessop, executive director of the London-based Caribbean Council for Europe, wrote earlier this month. "The principle thrust is that the industries that still underwrite the Caribbean's viability (bananas, sugar, rum, etc.) need to achieve a stable transition out of preferences."

Caricom will also consider a draft agreement to establish a Caribbean supreme court, as well as rules for the court and a code of judicial conduct. Guyana, Barbados and Jamaica have already decided to set up the court at the earliest possible date.

All but two of the independant members of Caricom, plus the British territory of Montserrat, still use the Privy Council in London as their final appeals court, a holdover from colonial days. However, regional leaders say it is time to establish a court reflecting the region's culture.
All Caricom states have maintained the death penalty, a popular measure at home that draws condemnation from the British government and human rights groups abroad.
Caricom will also review its relations with Washington, following the December 'narco-summit' in Antigua.

That meeting was sparked by comments from a senior U.S. state department official, who hinted that Jamaica faced decertification if it failed to sign a 'shiprider' accord that would allow U.S. lawmen to pursue suspected drug traffickers into Jamaica's airspace and waters.

All but two Caricom states -- Jamaica and Barbados -- have already signed such agreements, and Jamaican officials said earlier this month that talks with the United States on a shiprider agreement were proceeding "satisfactorily." Jamaica continues to insist, however, that it will not allow foreign agents to operate in its territorial waters or airspace.

Following the December narco-summit, Caricom requested a meeting with President Clinton to resolve the differences. Clinton is to visit Barbados on May 13, well after the March 1 deadline when he must submit to Congress a list of countries that are cooperating in drug matters, and those that should be decertified.
